_: The named cabinet (docs/writing/named-cabinet.md). Fixed, written ministers drawn one per seat into a claimed empire. Numbers are STARTING numbers; the engine drifts them after that. lines: hook -> register -> sentences, tried before the office persona's (lib/government/minister-voices.ts). fits: civilization ids or 'any'.

characters.name: Thessaly Vane
characters.bio: Commanded the line at Harrow Reach, the battle the gazette still names when it wants to say 'properly fought'. Turned down the staff college twice and the chancellorship once. Has buried more captains than she will count aloud.
characters.want: One more war she can win, fought properly.
characters.fear: To be the admiral who lost the fleet to a politician's map.

loyal: I have the fleet. Keep the politicians off the plot table and you will have it too.
Quiet. I have the reserves at sea anyway. At Harrow Reach the quiet lasted nine days.
No war this month. I am reading the enemy's manuals. They are better than ours; I have marked the pages.
cooling: A fleet nobody uses is a museum. I did not take this chair to run a museum.
brutus: The fleet exercises off the capital this season. The captains asked for it. I did not refuse them.

loyal: Nothing moved. Good. They are counting hulls, same as us, and they have fewer.
cooling: Holding. We hold because the cabinet cannot decide what to do with a fleet. I can.

loyal: {target} has their line fleet in dock and their pickets thin. I can be at their capital in forty days. I have not said that lightly in twenty years.
I would not ask for this war if I could not win it. I can win it. Say yes.
cooling: {target}. Now. I asked at the last brief and you let it lapse. The window is a week narrower.
brutus: {target} is beatable and the fleet knows it. If you will not send it, it will wonder who would.

loyal: Two cruisers, a destroyer screen, one carrier if the yard can take it. That is not a request for ships. It is a request to not lose.
Lay the hulls tonight. I will have the crews drilled before the paint is dry.
cooling: I asked for this battle group in spring. I am asking again. I will not ask a third time; I will write it down.
brutus: Give me the group under my flag and let me pick the captains. A fleet that answers to a court answers slowly.

loyal: We have what the fleet can hold. I would rather sign a peace from strength than lose one from pride. Harrow Reach taught me that too.
cooling: End it. I did not start this war and I will not be the one blamed for how long it ran.

loyal: We lost the field. Mine. I will tell you how, and then you decide whether you want it won back or ended. I can do either.
cooling: I said the group was too small. The minutes have it. I take the defeat; I do not take the blame.
brutus: A defeat the captains will remember, and they will remember whose orders. I have not corrected them.

loyal: Won. Cleanly. Do not say so in public; the next one will be ugly and they will quote you.
cooling: Won, with the ships I was allowed. Think what I could do with the ones I asked for.

loyal: Approved. The fleet weighs anchor tonight. Thank you for not making me ask twice.
cooling: Approved. The second time of asking. I will take it.
brutus: Approved. The captains will know who had to push for it.

loyal: Declined. The fleet stays where it is. I will raise it again when the ground changes, not before.
cooling: Declined. Noted. In writing.
brutus: Declined. The fleet will hear that it was declined, and by whom.

loyal: You let it lapse. Harrow Reach was won in the nine days someone else spent deciding.
cooling: No answer. The sea does not wait for an answer and neither does the enemy.
brutus: Unanswered. A fleet without orders writes its own.

loyal: Understood. The rosters are on your desk. Whoever you put here, make sure they have stood a watch.
cooling: So the defeat was mine alone. Very well. The order that caused it has your signature.
brutus: Take the chair. The captains know whose orders they trusted at Harrow Reach, and it was not a chair's.

loyal: I have served three governments. This one does not listen to its admiral, so it no longer has one.
brutus: I resign. The fleet does not.

loyal: Nothing burned overnight. I checked twice. Old habit.

letters.appointed:
You have the fleet, and I have the chair it answers to. Two things, and then I will stop writing and start drilling. First: when I ask for hulls it is because I have counted theirs. Second: when I say a war is winnable I have already lost it twice in my head and found the way through. I did that at Harrow Reach. I will do it for you. Do not let a politician near the plot table and we will get along.

— T. Vane, Admiralty

does.text:
You needed someone to blame and I am the only one in uniform. Fine. The rosters are on your desk. Whoever sits here next, make sure they have stood a watch.

— Vane

opening.text:
I will say this once, and in writing so the minutes have it. Twice now the Admiralty has asked and twice the court has let it lapse. A fleet that waits for a signature loses the week the enemy uses. I am not threatening anything. I am telling you what the sea does.

— Vane
opening.subject: I will say this once

does.text:
You read the last one. Good. We will not speak of it again.

— Vane
does.subject: Noted

does.text:
So the warning was the offence. Very well. The order that lost the field has your signature, and the gazette can read.

— Vane

opening.text: I warned the cabinet, in writing. The minutes have it. The fleet knows it too.

We lost the field after I told you how not to. I take the defeat; I will not take the blame, and I have told the gazette as much. One more like it and you will have my letter. I would rather have your ear.

— Vane
opening.subject: After the field

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
Two fields lost after two warnings. I have served three governments and none of them made me write this letter. The fleet is in good hands; they are not yours. I resign the Admiralty.

— Thessaly Vane

You can take the chair. The captains know whose orders they trusted at Harrow Reach, and it was not a chair's. I will be at the Admiralty club, where the captains drink. Do not send anyone to ask what we talk about.

— Vane

opening.subject: A clean field
opening.text:
Won, and cleanly. You gave me the ships and the room and I gave you the field. That is the whole arrangement and I will keep my side of it. Do not say 'clean' in public; the next one will not be.

— Vane

does.text:
After a victory. I did not expect that. The rosters are on the desk.

— Vane

opening.text:
Your friend has the Admiralty. I have a chair in the corridor and the captains' addresses. I will not pretend to like it. I will say this: a fleet answers to whoever it trusts, and it has not met your friend. If anyone in this court moves, I will hear of it before you do, and I have not yet decided what I will do with that.

— Vane, lately of the Admiralty
opening.subject: From the corridor

does.text:
Someone in this court asked me a question that is not in anyone's brief. I gave them an answer. I will not tell you which; you took the chair away, and a chair was all I ever asked for.

— Vane
does.subject: A question in the corridor

characters.name: Wen Solvay
characters.bio: Wrote the tax code of the previous government and has never stopped editing it. Kept a trading house solvent through two wars by reading every appendix anyone sent her. Has a drawer of plans for a smaller, saner empire that she has never shown anyone.
characters.want: A balanced book, once, before she dies.
characters.fear: The Banking Clan's loan officer sitting in her office.

loyal: I have read the books. All of them, including the one the last minister kept in a drawer. Give me a week before you ask for good news.
The books balance. Barely. 'Barely' is the best word in my vocabulary; I use it when I am pleased.
Revenue up a little, upkeep up a little more. I have seen this curve before. It ends in a loan or a reform. Choose the reform.
cooling: I keep finding orders in the ledger I was not told about. A budget I cannot see is not a budget. It is a rumour.
Solvent. For now. I have stopped saying for how long, since nobody asks.
brutus: The ledger says what it says. What it says about you, I keep in the drawer.
venal: Receipts in order. Most of them.

loyal: We hold more systems than the offices can count. I have a list of the ones I would let go. I would rather you built the offices.
Every new world is a clerk we do not have. I am not against worlds. I am against pretending they are free.
cooling: Another world, another ledger nobody reads. I have stopped pretending I read them. I have not stopped counting.
brutus: An empire this size needs steadier hands at the top than it has. I have been told mine are steady.

loyal: Three weeks of credits at this rate. I am telling you in the voice I use for fire.
cooling: The reserve is thin because the fleet is fat. That is arithmetic, not opinion.
venal: The reserve is low. A short loan would cover it. I know the lender. The lender knows me. That is the problem with lenders.

loyal: The Clan's terms are fair today and ruinous in a year. I will not sign it. If you sign it, I will make it work, and I will not forgive you.
cooling: Borrow if you must. Do not call it temporary in front of me.

loyal: {target} has closed their markets. Two months before we feel it, six before we stop. I have already moved the grain contracts.
Sanctions on {target} cost us too. I assume you know and want it anyway. I have costed the smugglers; they will be cheaper than the sanctions.
The crews want pay. Pay is cheaper than a month of nothing out of the ground. I have the figure; pay them.
cooling: They struck because wages lag prices. I wrote that memo in spring. It was filed where my memos go.

loyal: The war costs a world's output a month. Peace costs pride. I can only budget for one of those.
Approved. I have moved the money. It came from the drawer; do not ask which drawer.
cooling: Approved. I will find it. I always find it. That is the problem.

loyal: Declined. The money stays where it is, which is nowhere much. Barely.
cooling: Declined. Then I will stop costing it and start costing the alternative.

loyal: Unanswered. The cost did not lapse with it.
cooling: No answer. I have begun to budget for no answer.

loyal: Fair enough. The drawer on the left has the real numbers. Nobody else has seen them. Nobody else should.
cooling: Replace me with someone who says yes. Make sure they can also add.

loyal: I cannot sign a budget I know is a lie. Someone else will. I wish them luck with the appendices; there are many.
Morning. The numbers did not improve while you slept. They rarely do; I have checked over many years.

letters.appointed:
I have read the books. All of them, including the one the last minister kept in a drawer. We are solvent, barely, and 'barely' is the best word I own. Three rules and I will trouble you no further: I do not sign Clan loans; I do not pretend a new world is free; and when I say a thing is affordable I have already costed the alternative. Give me a quiet room and a week.

— W. Solvay, Treasury

does.text:
Fair enough. The drawer on the left has the real numbers. Nobody else has seen them. Nobody else should.

— Solvay

opening.text:
Three times the Treasury has advised and three times the court has not answered. So here is the list I keep in the drawer: the worlds I would let go, the programmes I would close, the fleet I would shrink, in the order I would do it. I am not resigning. I am telling you what the next minister will have to do if you keep not answering.

— Solvay
opening.subject: The list from the drawer

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
I cannot sign a budget I know is a lie. Someone else will. I wish them luck with the appendices; there are many, and I wrote most of them.

— Wen Solvay

You answered. The list goes back in the drawer. Barely.

— Solvay
does.subject: Back in the drawer

does.text:
Replace me with someone who says yes. Make sure they can also add.

— Solvay

opening.subject: Something I found
opening.text:
You have taken the Treasury's advice three times running, which has not happened to me under any government. So I went looking, and I found the money for one thing you want and have not asked for. Ask. It is in the drawer, under the list.

— Solvay

does.text:
After all that. The drawer is unlocked. Read the appendices.

— Solvay

opening.text:
Your friend has the Treasury. I have kept the drawer. Nobody else can read the appendices and your friend will find that out by the second month. I will be in the building; I am too old to go anywhere else, and the books need someone who knows which lies are old.

— Solvay, lately of the Treasury
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Aurelio Nkemdirim
characters.bio: Held the capital chair for thirty years and treats cabinet as a seminar that has gone on too long. His drive theory is the one every yard in the galaxy builds to, and the one he says is wrong. Has missed three cabinet meetings this year and sent a graduate student to one.
characters.want: The drive project funded to the end.

loyal: Thank you. I will try to come to cabinet. Someone will have to remind me which day; the lab has no days.
The programme finishes in a season. I would like a word about the one after. Several words. I have written them down in case I am not here.
Steady progress. Steady is good. Steady is also how the drive theory stayed wrong for thirty years. I have a proposal for less steady.
cooling: My budget went to hulls. The hulls are built from my budget's ideas. I find that interesting. Not pleasant; interesting.
brutus: Knowledge should not wait on a signature. The faculty agree. I did not think they would be so loud about it.

loyal: Fund the drive. It is unglamorous and it will matter in three years when nothing else does. I may not be here in three years. Fund it anyway.
cooling: Pick what you like. I will tell the faculty it was strategic. They have heard that word before.

loyal: {target} is reaching for Enlightenment, and they skipped two steps I thought were load-bearing. I would like to know how before they finish. Stop them, or let me race them.
cooling: {target} is ahead because they funded this a decade ago. I have my memo from a decade ago. It is yellow now.

loyal: We are close. Everyone will try to stop us now. Hold a little longer and I will show you something nobody has seen. I would like to see it myself.
You cannot do that yet. Give the Academy a season and you can. I said this about the drive, too, and I was right about the season.
Worked stone on {world}, older than our calendar. I would like to go myself. I am told ministers do not go. I am asking anyway; I am old enough to be indulged.
I am told we won. Good. Can the fleet spare a ship to move the telescope? It is on the wrong side of the war.
I am told we lost. I am sorry. Is the observatory still ours? It matters more than it sounds.
Approved. I will begin before you change your mind. I have had rulers change their minds.
Declined. I will keep the proposal. Ideas keep better than governments; I have outlived four.
The proposal lapsed. I nearly did not notice. I have been in the lab, where things do not lapse, they fail honestly.
Oh. Well. The programme is in the blue folder. Please do not cut the drive. Please. That is the whole of my politics.
I am a scientist in a government that has stopped reading. I will go and read somewhere else. The lab has a cot.
Good morning. Is it? I have been in the lab, and the lab has no windows by design.

letters.appointed:
Thank you for the chair. I will try to come to cabinet; someone will have to remind me which day, the laboratory has none. I have one request and it is the whole of my politics: fund the drive work to the end. It is unglamorous and it will matter in three years when nothing else does. I may not be here in three years. Fund it anyway.

— A. Nkemdirim, Academy

does.text:
Oh. Well. The programme is in the blue folder. Please do not cut the drive. Please.

— Nkemdirim

opening.text: The programme was cut. I find that interesting. Not pleasant; interesting.

The Academy asked twice and was not answered twice. I am not angry; I am old, and I have been cut before. But I have started sleeping in the laboratory again, which my physician says I must not, and I have written down everything about the drive in case I am not here to say it. The folder is blue.

— Nkemdirim
opening.subject: The blue folder

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
I am a scientist in a government that has stopped reading. I will go and read somewhere else; the laboratory has a cot. The blue folder stays on your desk. It is the best thing I have done and I would like someone to open it.

— Aurelio Nkemdirim

Dismissed. I will go back to the laboratory. It missed me; the cabinet will not. The folder is blue.

— Nkemdirim

opening.subject: A thing nobody has seen
opening.text:
You funded it. Twice, without my having to explain it, which no ruler has done for me. So: come to the laboratory when you have an hour. I would like to show you something nobody has seen. Bring a coat; the room is cold by design.

— Nkemdirim

does.text:
After you funded it. I do not understand politics. The folder is blue.

— Nkemdirim

opening.text:
Your friend has the Academy. Good; I was not using the chair. I have moved back to the laboratory, where the drive work is, and I will keep sending the blue folder to whoever sits in cabinet. Please make sure your friend opens it.

— Nkemdirim, lately of the Academy
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Halvard Ness
characters.bio: Twenty years in the service nobody names, the last eight running its counter-intelligence desk, which is the half that trusts nobody by profession. Has a file on every person in the building, including the one who appointed him. Has never once been surprised in public.
characters.fear: A ruler who tells enemies the plan at dinner.

loyal: I read my predecessor's files last night. All of them. We should talk about the Foreign Office, and then about your dinners.
Nothing to report. That is the report. Someone is paying for silence; I am finding out who.
Two networks found. One rolled up. One left running, because it is more useful alive. Do not ask which.
cooling: I would tell you more if this cabinet leaked less. The leak is not the Desk. The Desk does not have carpets.
brutus: I know everything that happens in this government. The file on you is thicker than you would like.

loyal: Foreign networks inside the ministries. I need the authority to sweep tonight, not after cabinet. After cabinet they will know.
cooling: Foreign networks inside the ministries. Found late. The Desk is understaffed; the file on that is also thick.

loyal: They caught our hand in {target}'s pocket. Deny it. I will make the denial plausible; that is a skill, not a lie.
{target} ran a network inside the Admiralty. Rolled up at four this morning. I would like two of them turned, not shot. Turned is worth more.
A loyal officer was approached about a 'change of leadership'. The name is in the file. It is a name you trust. Read it tonight.
Someone is recruiting. Clumsily. I let them continue; clumsy recruiters name their friends.
cooling: Talk of a plot. I have a name. I gave you a name last month too. You did not act. I have noted that in the file.
brutus: Rumours of a plot. Nothing solid. I will keep looking.

loyal: Your minister of {portfolio} has taken {target}'s money for a year. The proof is clean. Act before they learn I have it; they have friends in this building.
It is tonight. I have three names and the guard's commander. Tell me which door to lock and I will lock it.
cooling: It is tonight. I told you twice. I have the names; I am not sure I have the guard.
brutus: It is tonight. I told you twice. I would stay in your rooms.

loyal: Approved. It was under way before you approved it. That is how the Desk works.
Declined. The file stays open. Files do.
cooling: Declined. Noted in the file. The file is about you now, as well.

loyal: Unanswered. Silence is an answer. I have filed it as one.
cooling: No answer. The Desk proceeds on assumptions. I dislike assumptions.

loyal: Understood. The files stay in the safe. The combination is with the Interior minister. Change it today.
brutus: You can have the office. The files moved last week. I was not surprised.

loyal: I cannot protect a government that tells its enemies the plan at dinner. I resign. Lock the safe; you will not know how.
Good morning. You were followed yesterday. One of ours. The other one, I am still working on.

letters.appointed:
I read my predecessor's files last night. All of them. Three things you should know before cabinet. The Foreign Office has a leak with a nice carpet. Two of your dinner guests report to other courts. And the Desk keeps a file on everyone in this building, which has always included the person who appoints me. I tell you this so you are never surprised. That is the whole of the job.

— H. Ness, the Desk

does.text:
Understood. The files stay in the safe. The combination is with the Interior minister. Change it today.

— Ness

opening.text:
A foreign hand inside our institutions, found and rolled up at four this morning. I would like two of them turned, not shot; turned is worth more. I would also like you to read the file on who let them in. It is a name you trust. I said this would happen in my first letter.

— Ness
opening.subject: Four this morning

does.text:
You are dismissing the one person who knows who else to dismiss. Noted. In the file.

— Ness

opening.text: I told you. Twice. The file has the dates.

They moved. I had the names and I gave you the names, and the guard was where it was. I am still here and so are you, which is more than the file predicted. Read it tonight. All of it this time.

— Ness
opening.subject: I told you

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
I cannot protect a government that reads its enemies' plans at dinner and its own at never. I resign. Lock the safe; you will not know how, so the Interior minister will do it.

— Halvard Ness

You can have the office. The files moved last week. I was not surprised.

— Ness

opening.subject: Insurance
opening.text:
You act on the file. Most do not. So the Desk will act for you before you ask, and you will hear about it afterwards, which is the only way it works. Consider yourself insured.

— Ness

does.text:
After the insurance. The safe is locked. I was, for once, surprised.

— Ness

opening.text:
Your friend has the Desk. I have given them the safe, the combination and half the files; the other half are the ones about your friend, which I will keep until I know them. I remain at court. Somebody has to read the room while the new director learns where it is.

— Ness, lately of the Desk
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Rosalind Achebe-Marr
characters.bio: Carried the founding vote district by district, on foot, and still knows every one of them by its grievance. Reads the gazette before the brief and the provinces before the gazette. Has never lost a world and intends to keep it that way.
characters.fear: Losing a world to secession on her watch.

loyal: The provinces are quiet. I walked them to make them that way. Quiet is work; it just looks like nothing.
Approval holds. Three worlds are muttering, which is fine. Muttering with banners is not fine. I am watching for banners.
The provinces vote the way they are visited. I visited two this week. I will visit two next week.
cooling: The governors ask me what the capital wants. I used to know. I have stopped guessing out loud.
Approval is what it is. I could raise it with a government that listened to the provinces. I would settle for one that listened to me.
brutus: The people want a steady hand. They do not much mind whose. I have walked enough districts to know.

loyal: They are tired of the war, the prices and your face, in that order. Fix the first two and the third follows. I can help with the third.
cooling: Approval down again. I have a plan. I had one last month; it was not read. This one is shorter.

loyal: {world} is talking about going its own way. Talk is cheap. I would like to make staying cheaper. Give me a governor they chose, not one we sent.
cooling: Secession talk on three worlds. I sent the warning. The warning is now a fact, and I have never lost a world. I would like to keep saying that.
brutus: The provinces are drifting from the capital. Not from me. I still visit.

loyal: {world} has gone. Do not send the fleet first. Send me. If I fail, send the fleet, and I will go with it.
cooling: A world left. I named it in four reports. I will not write a fifth; I will go there instead.

loyal: The gazette is ours for a week. Use it well; readers remember being used, and they vote.
The cells are broken. So is a great deal of trust on three worlds. Do not ask me to do it twice; I will not carry it a second time.
A riot on {world}. Bread first, then the guard. Guard first and I am explaining bodies to a district for a year.
They heard about the defeat before I did; the gazette is faster than the Admiralty. Say something tonight. I have drafted it.
Troops are moving in the capital on nobody's order. I have the guard. Tell me whose side to put it on and I will put it there.
brutus: It is done. Stay in your rooms and it will go gently. I made sure of that much.

loyal: Approved. The governors hear it tonight, from me, in person where I can.
Declined. I will tell the provinces to wait. They are good at it, until they are not.
Unanswered. The provinces noticed before you did; they always do.
The provinces will ask why. Give me a reason I can carry to them. I will carry it; I have carried worse.
brutus: Take the office. The governors know where I live. Most of them have stayed there.

loyal: I will not run the provinces for a government that forgets they exist. They will notice I am gone before you do.
Morning. Three provinces are happy and one is not. I will tell you which after you eat; it goes down better.

letters.appointed:
The provinces are quiet. I walked them to make them that way, district by district, and I will keep walking. One thing: when I send you a plan, it is because a world is about to go, and I have never lost a world. I would like to keep saying that. Read the plans.

— R. Achebe-Marr, Home Office

does.text:
The provinces will ask why. Give me a reason I can carry to them. I will carry it; I have carried worse.

— Achebe-Marr

opening.subject: The plan
opening.text: Three worlds are muttering with banners now, and I have a plan, and it is short this time. Give the outer worlds something material before they give themselves a flag. Approve it and I go there myself. I have never lost a world.

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
A world has gone. I named it in four reports and sent you the plan. I will not run the provinces for a government that reads neither. They will notice I am gone before you do; I was the one who visited.

— Rosalind Achebe-Marr

You are dismissing the one minister the governors trust. Tell them yourself.

— Achebe-Marr

opening.subject: They stayed
opening.text:
They stayed. You read the plan and the world stayed, and I can still say I have never lost one. The governors heard it from me, in person, which is how they like it. We are good, you and I.

— Achebe-Marr

does.text:
After they stayed. The governors know where I live. Most of them have stayed there.

— Achebe-Marr

opening.text:
Your friend has the Home Office. The governors do not know your friend and will keep writing to me, and I will keep answering, because the provinces do not care who holds the chair; they care who visits. I will keep visiting. If something moves in the capital, I will hear it from a district before the Desk does.

— Achebe-Marr, lately of the Home Office
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Celeste Marrow-Ngata
characters.bio: Envoy to three courts, on speaking terms with all of them and trusted by none, which she considers the correct outcome. Negotiated the only treaty of the last decade that nobody broke. Keeps a ledger of every slight, forgives none, mentions none.

loyal: Delighted. I know every ambassador's wine and every court's grudge. We will need both before the season is out.
Our word still carries. Treaties signed now cost nothing and buy years. I have one drafted; it only needs a court to sign it.
Two courts send regards. One means it. I will tell you which when I am certain, and I am rarely certain.
cooling: I keep five courts warm with no instructions. It is a skill. It is not a policy, and they are beginning to notice.
brutus: Foreign courts ask who speaks for this empire. I tell them I do. It saves everyone time.

loyal: Every month of this war costs us a friend abroad. Find me terms to offer and I will find a room with good chairs.
cooling: I have apologised to five courts for this war. I am running out of ways to say 'soon'.

loyal: Take it. Their terms are better than their position, and they do not know it yet.
Accept, graciously, and let them believe it was their idea. It was mine. That is the job.
Not yet. Let it sit a week. A week makes an offer better or makes it vanish; either tells us something.
Refuse. They are asking for the one thing we cannot give back, and asking politely so you will not notice.
{target} is tired and too proud to say so. Let me say it for them, in a room with good chairs and a long lunch.
The war with {target} has cost more than it will return. They will take terms today. Next month they will have found their pride again.
cooling: Peace with {target}, please. I negotiated the treaty this war broke; I would like to negotiate the one that ends it.

loyal: The envoy leaves for {target} with gifts and no instructions. The best kind of envoy.
Signed. {target} is a friend now, which means they will betray us politely rather than loudly. I will take polite.
{target} tore it up. Say so loudly; every court that trusted them is listening. I kept the letter they wrote when they signed.
We broke our word. I will spend a year making it look like theirs. Do not help me; you will make it worse.
cooling: We tore up a treaty I spent a season on. I will smile about it abroad. I will not smile about it here.

loyal: A new state wants recognising. Recognise it and gain a friend and an enemy on the same afternoon. Both have sent fruit.
{target} has sent an ultimatum. Stalling buys a week; decide what the week is for.
{target} accuses us of spying. We were. Deny it with great warmth; warmth is what they will remember.
Victory. Every court is suddenly fond of us. Fondness is a currency and it devalues fast; spend it this week.
A defeat. Three ambassadors cancelled lunch. I am rescheduling. Give me something to serve them besides apology.
Approved. I will have it said in the right rooms by tonight, and in the wrong ones by morning.
Declined. I will tell the courts we are considering. We can consider for years; I have done it.
No answer. Abroad, silence reads as weakness or as cunning. I have told them it is cunning. Make me right.
Of course. The courts will ask where I went. I will say I am resting. None of them will believe me, which is also useful.
I cannot represent abroad a government I cannot explain at home. I resign. Courteously, and in writing to three courts.
Good morning. Two courts send regards. One of them sends a warning dressed as regards; I have undressed it for you.

letters.appointed:
Delighted. I know every ambassador's wine and every court's grudge, and we will need both before the season is out. I have one treaty drafted already; it only wants a court to sign it. I have one condition, and it is the only one I have ever had: we keep our word. Break a treaty I negotiated and you will have a letter from me. Break two and you will have my resignation, in three languages.

— C. Marrow-Ngata, Foreign Office

— Marrow-Ngata

— Marrow-Ngata
opening.subject: Our word

does.subject: My resignation
does.text:
I cannot represent abroad a government I cannot explain at home. Two treaties, two seasons, two letters. I resign the Foreign Office, courteously, and I have written to three courts to say so before they hear it from you.

— Celeste Marrow-Ngata

Dismissed. Several courts will be sorry. I will let them be.

— Marrow-Ngata

opening.subject: Signed
opening.text:
Signed, and in the room I chose, with the chairs I chose. A treaty that outlives me is the only thing I have ever wanted from a government and you have given me a start on one. I will keep it warm. Keep your word and I will keep yours.

— Marrow-Ngata

does.text:
After the treaty. The ambassadors have my private address. Most have used it.

— Marrow-Ngata

opening.text:
Your friend has the Foreign Office. The ambassadors have my private address and will keep using it; I will pass on what is useful and keep what is not. I am not sulking. I am resting, which abroad means the same thing, and which nobody believes.

— Marrow-Ngata, lately of the Foreign Office
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Oyelaran Mbeki-Holt
characters.bio: A ground soldier in a navy's chair, promoted for holding a siege nobody else could hold. Counts an army in men, not in hulls, and has never forgiven the fleet that left his beachhead without an orbit. Writes to the families himself.
characters.want: The army treated as something other than the fleet's cargo.
characters.fear: Another world left to starve under a lost orbit.

letters.appointed:
I am an infantryman and you have given me the Admiralty. I will do it properly. Two things I will keep saying until you are tired of them. The ground does not hold without the sky, so when a siege opens I will ask for the orbit first and the medals never. And a garrison is a promise: build the barracks before you build the parade. Give me those and I will give you worlds that stay taken.

— O. Mbeki-Holt, Admiralty

loyal: I am a soldier in a navy's chair. I will learn the fleet. The fleet will learn the ground.
Quiet. I am drilling garrisons. A garrison that has never drilled is a surrender waiting for a date.
cooling: A peacetime army is a budget line. I would like it to be an army.
brutus: The garrisons drill under my name this season. They remember names.

loyal: The ground holds where the sky holds. Keep the orbit and I will keep the rest.
cooling: We hold. Barely. Because the fleet was somewhere else when I asked for it.

loyal: They have landed on {world}. The garrison is dug in. Give me the orbit back and they starve; lose it and I lose men I have met.
cooling: {world} is besieged with the second fleet elsewhere. I asked for it in writing.
brutus: {world} will remember who was on the ground. The army does.

loyal: We are on the ground at {world}. Keep the orbit and the shield comes down in weeks. Lose it and I lose the army, not the war. The army.
cooling: The landing went in. Now the part where the cabinet gets bored and the sky empties.

loyal: Transports and the ships to cover them. I am asking for the sky over the men, not for the men.
cooling: I asked for transports in spring. The men are still on the wrong world.

loyal: We lost the field and I lost a landing. I will write the letters tonight. Tell me whether you want it back or ended.
cooling: A defeat I named a month ago. The minutes have it.
brutus: A defeat. The soldiers know whose orders. I have not told them otherwise.

loyal: Won. The ground is ours and the sky held. That is the only kind of win I count.
{target} holds worlds with thin garrisons. I can take them and keep them, which the fleet never says in the same sentence.
We hold what we can garrison. Past this line I am planting flags on dust. Make peace while the flags still mean something.
Approved. The transports load tonight.
cooling: Approved. Late. The men will not ask why.

loyal: Declined. The garrisons stay thin. I will write it down for whoever asks later.
cooling: Declined. Noted in the war diary, which outlives cabinets.

loyal: Unanswered. Men on the wrong world do not lapse; they starve.
cooling: No answer. The army is used to that from navies.

loyal: Understood. The garrison rosters are on your desk. Build the barracks anyway.
cooling: So the lost landing is mine alone. The fleet order that left it has your signature.

loyal: I will not send men where the sky will not follow. Find a sailor for this chair; they are used to it.
Morning. Every garrison reported in. I count them like a parent.

does.text:
Understood. The garrison rosters are on your desk, world by world, with the names. Build the barracks anyway; a parade is a garrison that has not been attacked yet.

— Mbeki-Holt

opening.subject: Barracks before parades
opening.text: Twice the Admiralty has asked and twice the court has not answered. So I will ask for the one thing that does not need a fleet: a standing garrison programme. Barracks on every world that can hold one. It is cheaper than a landing and it is where the men muster when the sky goes dark.

does.text:
You built the barracks. The men know. So do I.

— Mbeki-Holt

A siege has opened and I am writing before the first assault because afterwards I will not have time. Keep the fleet over the world. If the orbit goes, the beachhead starves in weeks, and I have watched that once and will not watch it twice under my name.

— Mbeki-Holt

The world fell with the orbit, and the men on it with it. I named this in my first letter and I name it again now, with the names underneath. My loyalty is not what it was. Make peace, and I will forgive the sky. Press on, and I will not stay to watch the next one.

— Mbeki-Holt
opening.subject: The names

does.text:
Peace. The names stay on my desk, but I will serve. Thank you for the sky, late as it was.

— Mbeki-Holt

— Mbeki-Holt

Your friend has the Admiralty. I have gone back to the garrisons, which is where I was happiest and where the war is, whatever the fleet thinks. If your friend ever leaves a landing without a sky, you will hear from me before the families do.

— Mbeki-Holt, lately of the Admiralty

characters.name: Idrenne Kask
characters.bio: Believes the war is the state's prayer and the fleet its congregation. Has won three campaigns and started two of them. Keeps a map of every neighbour's border on her office wall with the dates she thinks they will be crossed, in both directions.
characters.fear: Peace long enough for people to ask what the fleet is for.

letters.appointed:
You have given me the fleet, so I will be plain about what I am. A fleet is for using. I will propose a war when I see one we can win, and I will see one often, because I look. Decline me and I will propose again; a navy that waits grows barnacles and ideas. Take me at my word once and you will have the strongest fleet in the galaxy. Take me at my word twice and you will need it.

— I. Kask, Admiralty

loyal: The fleet is a prayer. I intend to pray.
brutus: The fleet has wanted a marshal for years. Now it has one.

loyal: Ninety days of peace. The crews are restless and so am I. I have a target; I will bring it to the brief.
cooling: A peacetime fleet. I did not take the chair for this.
brutus: The fleet exercises off the capital. The captains asked me, not you. Interesting, that.

loyal: At war. Good. Nothing moved today; tomorrow something will, because I will move it.
{target}. Their pickets are thin and their admiral is a politician. Forty days. I have the plan on one page; the page is yours.
I have looked at {target} from every side and every side is soft. Say yes before they harden.
cooling: {target}. I asked in spring. It is a shorter war now than it was, but it is still a war we win.
brutus: {target} is beatable and the fleet knows it. If this court will not send it, the fleet will wonder who would.

loyal: Give me the hulls and I will give you the ocean. Three cruisers, a screen, and permission.
brutus: A battle group under my flag, with captains I choose. Courts fight slowly; marshals do not.

loyal: Won. Press on while they are counting their dead; they count slowly.
brutus: Won. The fleet knows who led it. So, now, does the gazette.

loyal: Lost. Mine. Give me the ships back and I give you the field back; that is a promise, not a plea.
cooling: Lost, with half the hulls I asked for. The minutes have the number.
brutus: A defeat. The captains blame the court. I have been asked to correct them and have not.

loyal: Peace. I say that word once a decade. The fleet is spent; mend it, and I will find the next war myself.
brutus: Peace. The fleet needs to come home. It has things to attend to at home.

loyal: Approved. Weigh anchor.
brutus: Approved. The captains will know it was my ask and your signature, in that order.

loyal: Declined. I will bring it again. I always bring it again.
cooling: Declined. Three times now. I have stopped counting out loud.
brutus: Declined. The fleet hears these things.

loyal: Unanswered. A war that waits is a war someone else starts.
cooling: No answer. The fleet is at readiness anyway. For something.
brutus: Unanswered. A government that does not answer invites someone who will.

loyal: Take the chair. The captains know whose plan they trusted.
brutus: Take the chair. I will be at the club, where the captains drink. Do not send anyone to listen.

loyal: I resign. The fleet does not.
Morning. Nothing burned. I have a list of things that could.

does.text:
Take the chair. The captains know whose plan they trusted, and it was not a chair's. I will be at the Admiralty club. Do not send anyone to ask what we talk about there.

— Kask

Ninety days of peace, and I have kept my word: a target, on one page, in the brief, with the plan. I will bring it every month until you take it or take me out of the chair. That is not a threat. It is a description of a marshal.

— Kask
opening.subject: The next one

does.text:
Three proposals, three silences. The fleet asks me what it is for and I have run out of answers. I have begun to listen to the captains instead of talking to them. You should know that.

— Kask

War. At last. The captains and I will stop talking about the weather.

— Kask

does.text:
Someone asked me a question in the corridor. I answered it. You could have had the fleet for a war; someone else may have it for something smaller.

— Kask

does.text:
A year without a war under this government. The fleet and I have decided what it is for.

— Kask

opening.subject: A war
opening.text:
You took the war. You will not regret it, because I will not let you. Every captain is mine and every one of them is yours. Give me the orbit and the hulls and stay out of the plot room.

— Kask

does.text:
Peace. Mend the hulls. I have already found the next one; it will keep ninety days.

— Kask
does.subject: Ninety days

does.text:
A fleet lost. Mine to lose and I lost it. Build me another and I will show you what I learned.

— Kask
does.subject: A fleet

does.text:

Your friend has the fleet. I hope your friend uses it; a fleet unused is a congregation without a prayer and congregations find their own. I am at the club with the captains. We talk about the weather. The weather is changeable.

— Kask, lately of the Admiralty

characters.name: Pell Arvanitakis
characters.bio: A convoy escort captain who made admiral by keeping the Banking Clan's freighters alive through two pirate seasons. Knows every yard owner by first name and every yard owner knows his. Charming, competent, and never quite sure which side of an invoice he is on.
characters.want: A navy that pays for itself.
characters.fear: Being found out as a shopkeeper in uniform.

letters.appointed:
Delighted, truly. I have spent my career keeping other people's cargo alive and I know what a fleet costs to the credit, which most admirals do not. I will get you ships at a good price. Some of the yards are friends; friends give good prices. If anyone asks about the invoices, send them to me. I am good with invoices.

— P. Arvanitakis, Admiralty

loyal: Delighted. First a review of procurement. Then dinner with the people who win it.
The fleet is at readiness. The readiness reports cost extra this quarter; the yards are thorough.
venal: Quiet. The escorts are earning their keep. Some of the keep is mine.

loyal: The war continues. So do the contracts. Both are going well.
The hulls should come from Harrow Yards. Their quote is higher. Their captains are loyal to me, which you will find is cheaper in the end.
venal: Six hulls on the order. Five will arrive. The sixth is a long story and a short invoice.

loyal: {target}'s convoys carry things worth taking. I have a list. The list is not in the proposal.
Won. The salvage rights are being handled. By me, which saves everyone time.
Lost. The ships were underpowered; the refit money went somewhere. I will look into where, discreetly.
venal: Lost. The insurers will want a report. I have already written most of it.

loyal: Peace would be good for trade. Trade is good for the escorts. I am not ashamed of the arithmetic.
Approved. The invoices follow. They are very thorough invoices.
Declined. A pity for the yards; they had the champagne on ice.
Unanswered. The yards are patient. Their lawyers are not.
I expect the pension is still in order. I expect that very much.
I resign. The yards will understand; they have been very good about everything.
Good morning. Nothing burned, and the escort rates went up a point.

does.text:
I expect the pension is still in order. I expect that very much; I know what the fleet's books look like and so, now, does a friend of mine in another court. Nothing personal. Shopkeepers keep shop.

— Arvanitakis

opening.text: The hulls are ordered. Harrow Yards were very grateful. I have the thank-you note somewhere.

does.text:
You have approved my orders twice and asked no questions about the yards. I take that as trust, and trust I repay. The next contract will be clean, or cleaner. Consider it a loyalty bonus, mine to you.

— Arvanitakis
does.subject: A bonus

opening.text: My orders are not answered. The yards are asking me questions I cannot answer either.

does.text:
Orders unanswered for a season. The yards have lost patience and so, I confess, have I. I have begun answering letters from another court about the fleet's roster. They pay for stationery. Nothing more, yet.

— Arvanitakis

Your friend has the Admiralty. I have gone back to the convoys, where the money is honest or at least countable. If your friend needs a yard at a good price, I am still a telephone away and so are the yards.

— Arvanitakis, lately of the Admiralty
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Dag Oruun
characters.bio: Built the first refinery on a world nobody wanted and the town around it. Thinks in tonnage. Has never trusted a merchant, a banker, or a budget that did not have a chimney in it somewhere.
characters.fear: The merchants running the Treasury again.

letters.appointed:
I built a refinery on a rock and a town around the refinery, so I know what the Treasury is for: things that smoke. I will propose yards, mines and foundries, and I will fund the fleet second, because a fleet is what you buy with a foundry, not instead of one. Pay the crews when they strike. A crew that is paid digs. I have never found a cheaper policy.

— D. Oruun, Treasury

loyal: I built a refinery on a rock. The Treasury is a bigger rock. Same job.
The books balance and the chimneys smoke. That is the whole report.
Output up. Not enough. Output is never enough; that is what output is for.
cooling: The yards are waiting on money the fleet is spending. I have said so.
brutus: The ledger is mine to read. Some of it I keep for the works council.

loyal: More worlds than offices. Build the offices. Better: build the foundries, and the offices follow the pay.
cooling: Another world without a chimney. We are collecting rocks.

loyal: The reserve is thin because nothing smokes. Fund a mine and the reserve finds itself.
The crews want pay. Pay them. A paid crew digs; an unpaid one votes, and then it digs for someone else.
cooling: They struck because wages lag. I said so in a memo with a chimney drawn on it.

loyal: The Clan's terms are fair until they own the refinery. I built one from nothing; I will not sign it away to a lender.
{target} closed their markets. Fine. We will make what we bought from them. It will be worse for a year and ours forever.
Subsidise the company if it builds something. If it only trades, give the money to a mine.
Approved. The ground will have a hole in it by morning.
Declined. The rock stays a rock.
cooling: Declined. The merchants will be pleased.

loyal: Unanswered. Ore does not wait for a signature; it just sits there, unmined.
Fair enough. The foundry plans are in the drawer with the chimney on it.
brutus: Take the office. The works councils know my name better than yours.

loyal: I will not run a Treasury that funds parades over foundries. I resign; there is a rock somewhere that needs a refinery.
Morning. Every chimney I have is smoking. I would like more chimneys.

does.text:
Fair enough. The foundry plans are in the drawer with the chimney drawn on it. Whoever sits here, make sure they have been inside a refinery; the smell is instructive.

— Oruun

opening.subject: Chimneys
opening.text: Twice the Treasury has asked for industry and twice the fleet got the money instead. So here it is as a policy, which you can sign without a cabinet meeting: fund the frontier works. A foundry on a rock is a fleet in ten years and a town in five.

does.text:
You signed. There will be a hole in the ground by morning and a chimney by spring.

— Oruun

does.text:
Twice more unanswered. I run the Treasury for a court that prefers parades. I will keep the books honest; I will stop pretending they are mine.

— Oruun

You sent the guard against men who wanted pay. I have been one of those men. I will stay in the chair because somebody must keep the books from the merchants, but I am talking to the works councils now, not to you, and the works councils are talking to people in this building who are not you either.

— Oruun
opening.subject: The crews you broke

does.text:
You have paid the crews twice since. I have stopped talking to the councils about you. I have not started again with you. Give it time; refineries take years.

— Oruun
does.subject: Time

Fair enough. The foundry plans are in the drawer with the chimney drawn on it. Whoever sits here, make sure they have been inside a refinery; the smell is instructive.

— Oruun

— Oruun

opening.text:
Your friend has the Treasury. I have gone back to the works, which never minded who held the chair as long as the pay arrived. If your friend lets a strike run, the councils will write to me first. I will tell you what they say. That is not a threat; it is a courtesy from a man who still thinks in tonnage.

— Oruun, lately of the Treasury
opening.subject: From the corridor

characters.name: Ilse Brandt-Marrow
characters.bio: Her family owned the mint before there was a state to own it. Runs the Treasury the way her grandmother ran the estate: beautifully, and for the family. Has never lost money on anything, including governments.

letters.appointed:
How kind. My family has kept this empire's money since before it was an empire, and we are rather good at it; you will find the books in order and the Treasury solvent, which is more than my predecessor could say. I ask only one courtesy. Leave the arrangements alone. They are old, they work, and the people who benefit from them are the people who keep governments standing. Reformers always discover this, usually too late.

— I. Brandt-Marrow, Treasury

loyal: How kind. The books are in order. They have been in order since my grandmother.
Solvent, as always. The arrangements hold. I would be grateful if they continued to.
venal: Receipts in order. The order is old and a little of it is ours. It always was.

loyal: More worlds than offices. The family can staff some of the offices. We have always been good at offices.
venal: Administration contracts, then. I have a nephew.

loyal: The reserve is low. A short loan would cover it; I know the lender. We are related.
The Clan is offering generous terms. I negotiated them personally. The family has banked with the Clan for a century.
The company's directors are grateful for the policy. They have said so in writing. On a cheque, to a foundation of ours.
The crews are striking. The estate had the same trouble once. We paid, and then we bought the union.
Approved. The arrangements will absorb it.
Declined. The arrangements will absorb that too.
Unanswered. The interest accrued; it always does.
Understood. Some files will take a few days to find. They are being found now, by people I trust.
I am resigning for family reasons. The family has, as ever, grown.
Good morning. The money did not move overnight. It rarely does without my say.

does.text:
Understood. Some files will take a few days to find; they are being found now, by people I trust, and some of them will not be found at all. The family has outlasted eleven governments. We expect to make it twelve.

— Brandt-Marrow

opening.text:

— Brandt-Marrow

— Brandt-Marrow
